nodes.title: Hodge–Deligne systems
nodes.statement: Fix a number field K, an embedding K→C, a smooth geometrically connected K-variety X with smooth model 𝓧/O_K[S⁻¹], and a rational prime p below no place of S, unramified in K, with v|p. A Hodge–Deligne system consists of a finite-rank Q local system on X(C), a continuous Q_p local system on 𝓧[1/p], a filtered finite locally free bundle with integrable connection on X, and a filtered F-isocrystal on the v-adic tube, with Betti–étale, Betti–de Rham, crystalline–de Rham and structural O B_cris comparisons. These preserve tensor operations, connection, filtrations and a finite weight filtration W. Require regular singularities, Griffiths transversality and fibrewise pure Hodge and Weil-weight conditions on gr_W. Rational Weil numbers need not be integral; polarization and a Z-lattice are additional conditions.
proofSteps: Use the supplied local systems, connections and F-isocrystals; form the category of tuples with the four actual comparison isomorphisms.
Impose finite filtrations, transversality, regularity and purity fibrewise; identify all comparison diagrams, including the structural period-sheaf connection.
acceptance: All four realizations have the same rank.
Do not infer a polarization or an integral lattice from the basic definition.

sources.match: The definition couples Betti, p-adic étale, filtered de Rham and crystalline data through comparison isomorphisms, with common weight filtrations and fibrewise purity conditions.

nodes.title: Integral and polarized systems
nodes.statement: For a Hodge–Deligne system, integral means a locally constant finite free Z lattice in its Betti realization spanning it over Q. Polarized means pure of a specified weight and equipped with a flat rational bilinear polarization of its variation of Hodge structure. Integral Frobenius means that, at every relevant closed point away from S and p and in the crystalline realization, Frobenius eigenvalues are algebraic integers. These are three separate predicates; integral Frobenius is not preserved by arbitrary duals.
proofSteps: Transport the lattice and pairing through the comparison maps without conflating a rational polarization with integrality of the pairing.
State integral Frobenius using the integral Weil predicate supplied by DWP.0.
acceptance: The category of all systems remains dual-closed; its integral-Frobenius subcollection need not be.

sources.match: These definitions add a Betti lattice, a pure polarization and algebraic integrality of Frobenius eigenvalues as distinct conditions on the preceding system.

nodes.title: Tensor category of compatible systems
nodes.statement: Over the fixed connected base of M2.0, morphisms are maps of all four realizations compatible with W, F, connection, Frobenius and all comparisons. With componentwise tensor products, duals, direct sums and the unit, Hodge–Deligne systems form a Q-linear neutral Tannakian category under evaluation of the Betti realization at a chosen complex point. Prove strictness of the filtrations and that the componentwise kernels and cokernels again satisfy the axioms; do not treat arbitrary filtered vector spaces as an abelian category.
proofSteps: Use strictness of Hodge morphisms and the exact admissible realization functors to construct kernels and cokernels with their comparisons.
Use geometric connectedness for faithfulness of fibre evaluation; verify rigidity and End(unit)=Q before invoking MC.6.
acceptance: On a disconnected base a fibre on one component is not a faithful functor on all components.

sources.match: Compatible realization maps define morphisms; the lemma establishes a neutral Tannakian category using a Betti fibre functor. Its proof uses strict Hodge morphisms.

nodes.title: Constant arithmetic systems
nodes.statement: A constant Hodge–Deligne system on 𝓧 is a pullback of a system over Spec O_K[S⁻¹]. The trivial coefficient system O_E for a finite-dimensional Q-algebra E has constant Betti E, trivial arithmetic Galois action on E⊗Q_p, trivial connection and degree-zero Hodge filtration, and Frobenius 1_E⊗σ_v. A constant arithmetic system may have nontrivial arithmetic Galois action; constancy here means trivial geometric variation.
proofSteps: Pull back the four realizations and the comparison maps from the arithmetic point.
Distinguish this pullback construction from the particular trivial coefficient unit.
acceptance: Geometric monodromy is trivial for every constant system.

nodes.title: Geometric cohomology and projectors
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective morphism f:Y→X extending smoothly and projectively over the model, construct the compatible system R^k f_*Q using Betti, étale, algebraic de Rham and crystalline cohomology. A compatible finite-group idempotent in the rational endomorphisms cuts out a direct-summand system; intersect its rational Betti image with an integral cohomology lattice modulo torsion to obtain a spanning lattice. Pure cohomological systems are polarized and have integral Frobenius eigenvalues. The general coefficient pushforward in LS Example 5.10 additionally requires a relative coefficient-comparison theorem, recorded as a gap rather than inferred from constant coefficients.
proofSteps: Construct the four usual cohomology objects and use the supplied proper comparison maps, including connection and filtration compatibility.
Use the algebraic finite-group action to identify the same projector in each realization; inherit purity and restrict a positive polarization to the summand.
acceptance: A rational projector need not preserve the original integral lattice; intersection, not integral application of the projector, constructs the new lattice.

sources.locator: Example 5.10, p. 43; proof of Lemma 5.29, pp. 49–51

nodes.title: Differential monodromy from a tensor generator
nodes.statement: Let V be a system on a smooth geometrically connected X/K with chosen K-rational fibre point, or after a stated finite extension supplying one. Define G_mon as the tensor automorphism group of the fibre functor on the rigid abelian tensor category generated by (V_dR,∇). Regular-singular Riemann–Hilbert identifies its base change to C with the Zariski closure of Betti geometric monodromy on V. Transport between fibre choices is by the tensor-isomorphism torsor, so the resulting groups are defined up to inner identification; no unrelated Picard–Vessiot theory is developed.
proofSteps: Use neutral reconstruction on the tensor category generated by the regular connection.
Apply exact tensor Riemann–Hilbert and the tensor-invariant characterization of the Zariski closure; descend the tensor category over K.
acceptance: Specify the finite extension if X(K) is empty; do not silently choose a K-rational base point.

sources.match: The group is reconstructed from the connection-generated tensor category and is compared over C with the algebraic closure of topological monodromy.

nodes.statement: On a smooth v-adic residue disk Ω of a system, parallel transport of its convergent F-isocrystal identifies all underlying crystalline pairs with one finite-dimensional (V,φ), with φ semilinear for the residue Frobenius. Use the horizontal crystalline–de Rham comparison to transport the varying filtration into a fixed flag space.

It is étale when its Betti Q-algebra is finite étale. In the arithmetic argument require E to be constant in the arithmetic-pullback sense. Its étale realization can have a nontrivial finite Galois permutation action.
proofSteps: Use the tensor category for multiplication and unit and impose the algebra identities in each realization.
Define étaleness through the Betti algebra and transfer it through the comparisons.
acceptance: Separate finite étale algebras from arbitrary finite-dimensional commutative algebras.

nodes.title: Finite étale coefficient operations
nodes.statement: Construct H⁰-algebras from the trivial algebra O_E, the rational group algebra Q[B] of a finite abelian group B, the convolution dual of the function algebra on a finite étale commutative group scheme, R⁰ of a proper smooth family, and pushforward along a finite étale base map. In the finite-monodromy case define crystalline realization by D_cris of the actual Galois representation. If K_v/Q_p is unramified of degree f, its semilinear Frobenius satisfies φ^f equal, under the unramified comparison, to the representation action of geometric Frobenius; the naive formula using the same residue-Frobenius action on both factors is not imposed.
proofSteps: Use group multiplication for the convolution dual, ordinary multiplication or cup product for the other algebra structures, and finite étale pushforward for descent.
Construct the crystalline component through the invariants functor, then compute its f-th iterate rather than prescribing a false semilinear formula.
acceptance: Check geometric versus arithmetic Frobenius once against the conventions of DWP.0 and use the chosen geometric action consistently.

nodes.statement: An E-module system is a system V with a unital action E⊗V→V compatible with the four realizations. A bilinear pairing valued in an invertible rank-one E-module L is E-balanced when B(ev,w)=B(v,ew).

Verify each comparison descends to the coequalizer and use finite étale semisimplicity for exactness.

Use the realization comparisons to transport the common rank.

Isomorphisms include the compatible similitude on L. Keep the whole orthogonal similitude group, which need not be connected.

Define isomorphisms of paired modules and identify the split standard automorphism groups after choosing bases.

Descent includes both Galois transport of the torsion character and cyclotomic transport of its values; a primitive character need not define a rank-one Q system.

Identify its origin-normalized character summands with SC.0, keeping the cyclotomic coefficient action.

nodes.title: Galois-orbit cohomology systems
nodes.statement: Let Y⊂X_K×A be a smooth projective family of hypersurfaces, X smooth over Q with suitable integral model and O_K[S⁻¹] finite étale over Z[S′⁻¹]. Let I be a finite orbit of pairs (ι,χ) under Gal(Q̄/Q)×Gal(Q^cyc/Q), with χ of order r prime to p, for which twisted cohomology vanishes outside degree n−1. Construct a constant finite étale H⁰-algebra E_I on X with geometric idempotents indexed by I, and an E_I-module system V_I whose geometric coefficient fibres are R^(n−1)f_(ι)*g_(ι)^*L_χ. Its E_I-rank is N=n!d when d=[H]^n/n!, and its Q-rank is |I|N. It is integral, pure polarized of weight n−1, and integral-Frobenius.
proofSteps: Construct both algebra and cohomology as compatible rational idempotent summands of finite étale multiplication-cover pushforwards.
Descend the orbit of idempotents together with the cyclotomic action; compute ranks on the geometric splitting cover.
Intersect with a cohomology lattice, restrict the geometric polarization, and inherit integral Frobenius on direct summands.
acceptance: The algebra has rank |I|; simply pushing forward the cyclotomic field along K/Q can have the wrong rank.

All translation and coefficient descent data must be carried along; the original pairing that couples χ and χ⁻¹ is not itself asserted E-bilinear.

Check the translated inversion squares to the identity, the coefficient balancing identity, parity and Galois descent.

nodes.title: Semilinear coefficient normalizers
nodes.statement: Let E/E₀ be finite étale in characteristic zero, V free of E-rank N>0, and H=GL_N, GSp_N or GO_N in its standard representation (with a perfect E-valued form after a line trivialization in the paired cases). Set B=Res_(E/E₀)H and G=N_(GL_(E₀)(V))(B). Identify G with invertible E-semilinear maps, respecting the form up to a semilinear similitude in the paired cases. Obtain 1→B→G→Aut_(E₀)(E)→1 as a group-scheme exact sequence, surjective fppf-locally. B is not renamed the identity component when H=GO_(2r).
proofSteps: After splitting E, recover its scalar algebra from the centralizer of the standard B action; a normalizing map must permute the coefficient factors.
Identify the normalizer of the classical form on each factor and descend; construct local lifts of coefficient permutations.
acceptance: Exactness is a scheme/functor statement, not an unsupported claim that every rational-point sequence is surjective.

nodes.title: Semilinear Frobenius centralizer bound
nodes.statement: In the preceding setup, if σ∈Aut_(E₀)(E) has fixed algebra E^σ=E₀ and φ∈G is σ-semilinear, then dim Z_G(φ)≤dim H. More generally on each σ-cycle of geometric coefficient factors, projection of Z_B(φ) to any one factor is injective, so the bound is one factor dimension per cycle.
proofSteps: Split E over an algebraic closure; fixed algebra E₀ means one permutation cycle.
The commuting equations propagate every component from one component around the cycle; the remaining equation restricts that component.
Pass from Z_B to Z_G through the finite component quotient.
acceptance: For σ=id on a split d-factor algebra the fixed-algebra hypothesis fails and a bound independent of d is false.

sources.match: When the coefficient automorphism has the ground field as fixed algebra, its semilinear centralizer has dimension at most one classical factor. The split-cycle proof gives the more general cyclewise formulation.

nodes.title: Semisimplification in the coefficient normalizer
nodes.statement: For the specific normalizer G of M2.2 and a subgroup Γ⊂G over a characteristic-zero field, use Richardson parabolics P_λ={g:lim_(t→0)λ(t)gλ(t)⁻¹ exists}, their Levi quotients and unipotent radicals. Γ is G-completely reducible when every such P_λ containing Γ has a Levi containing Γ. Projecting Γ from a minimal containing P_λ to its Levi gives a G-completely reducible subgroup, unique up to G-conjugacy after the source-qualified field extension. For Γ a representation image call this its G-semisimplification. Rational conjugacy and continuity require separate descent, not merely geometric closed-orbit uniqueness.
proofSteps: Import the dynamic parabolic and Levi construction, and the common connected complete-reducibility/closed-orbit input.
Specialize minimal-parabolic projection to the finite-component coefficient normalizer; prove conjugacy and continuity in the field cases consumed here.
Check that an element and its image in a Levi have conjugate semisimple parts and that tori in P are unipotently conjugate into a Levi.
acceptance: GL-semisimplification of the standard module agrees with the ordinary representation semisimplification.

nodes.statement: For an affine algebraic group G/k and a k-linear tensor category C with a fibre functor ω, a G-object is an exact faithful k-linear symmetric monoidal functor Rep_fd(G)→C together with a tensor trivialization of its composite with ω to the forgetful functor. Changing the trivialization conjugates the resulting homomorphism of Tannaka groups. A faithful representation with defining tensors describes the same structure only after proving the tensor reconstruction comparison.
proofSteps: Use Rep_fd(G) from the existing group-representation theory; define the structured exact tensor functor and chosen trivialization.
Use neutral reconstruction to recover the homomorphism of fibre groups.

nodes.title: Tensor filtrations and cocharacters
nodes.statement: For G in characteristic zero with reductive identity component, a G-filtration is an exact tensor-compatible filtration of the forgetful functor Rep_fd(G)→Vect, with the canonical associated-graded tensor structure. A splitting cocharacter μ gives F^aV=⊕_(j≥a)V_j. Two cocharacters define the same filtration precisely when their dynamic parabolics agree and they are conjugate in that parabolic. Restriction to G° identifies G-filtrations with G°-filtrations, but a parabolic alone records a filtration only up to indexing. On descending filtrations gr^a=F^a/F^(a+1).
proofSteps: Apply tensor-filtration splitting and compare its stabilizer and graded kernel with the existing dynamic parabolic and radical.
Use that cocharacters lie in G° and compare their associated filtrations, retaining their weights.
acceptance: Filtered vector spaces are an exact filtered category here; no claim makes all of them an abelian category.

nodes.title: Crystalline tensor structures and inner forms
nodes.statement: For a crystalline G-valued local Galois representation over Q_p with G in the preceding class, D_cris applied as an exact tensor functor gives filtered φ-data with an inner form G′ and a G′-filtration. A homomorphism G₁→G₂ induces a homomorphism between the corresponding inner forms, compatible with tensors. In the coefficient-normalizer case identify G′ with the de Rham coefficient normalizer through the actual realization comparison. There is no canonical equality G′=G for an arbitrary G-object.
proofSteps: Use exactness, faithfulness and tensor/dual compatibility of D_cris on crystalline representations.
Compare the two fibre functors through their tensor-isomorphism torsor; identify the induced group as the twist by this torsor.
In the standard coefficient representation use the given coefficient action and pairing to recognize the de Rham group.

nodes.title: Adjoint Hodge profiles and top-weight sums
nodes.statement: Given a G-filtration on a characteristic-zero group, define h^a=dim gr^a Lie(G), a finitely supported sequence of natural numbers. In the polarized weight-zero adjoint case h^a=h^(−a). Put D=Σ_a h^a, A=Σ_(a>0)h^a, B=Σ_(a>0)a h^a. Order the D weights with multiplicities nonincreasingly as w₁,…,w_D. For real x∈[0,D], define T(x)=Σ_(j≤floor x)w_j+(x−floor x)w_(floor x+1), with T(D)=Σ_j w_j. Thus T is continuous piecewise linear, with each weight appearing h^a times; it does not sum the multiplicities themselves.
proofSteps: Take the Lie-algebra filtration, its finite associated graded and multiplicities.
Define its decreasing weighted list and interpolate partial sums; retain a finite real domain for T.
acceptance: All arguments of T in a numerical criterion must lie in [0,D].

sources.match: Adjoint graded dimensions define a finite symmetric multiplicity profile; the piecewise-linear partial-sum function records the largest weights, including repetitions.

nodes.title: Uniform coefficient filtrations
nodes.statement: For a filtration of a coefficient-normalizer object, uniform means that the adjoint Hodge profile on H is the same at every geometric embedding of its finite étale coefficient algebra. If [E:E₀]=d, its restriction-of-scalars profile is d times the single-factor profile; in particular T_Res(dx)=dT_H(x). The numerical inequalities of the non-density theorem always use h_H,T_H, not the scaled restriction-of-scalars profile.
proofSteps: Split the coefficient algebra, compare each factor filtration and sum Lie-algebra graded dimensions.
Apply repetition of the ordered weight list for the T scaling.
acceptance: Uniformity is a factorwise condition and does not follow just from equidimensionality.

nodes.title: Finiteness of global coefficient-group types
nodes.statement: Fix p, a finite T containing p, and the coefficient normalizer G/Q_p of M2.2 with its fixed faithful standard representation and coefficient permutation action. Fix rank and an integer pure Weil weight w≥0. Continuous G-completely reducible representations G_Q→G(Q_p), unramified outside T and having characteristic polynomials in Z[t] with weight-w roots at Frobenius outside T, form finitely many G(Q_p)-conjugacy classes. Rational-orbit descent and the possibly disconnected GO coefficient group require the inputs recorded as gaps. This target extends the parent GL finiteness theorem; it is not inferred from finite GL-conjugacy classes alone.
proofSteps: Use bounded component degree and Hermite–Minkowski to restrict to finitely many extensions killing the component action.
Use the connected reductive refinement of the parent GL finiteness argument; conjugacy rigidity for a finite component group follows from vanishing of its characteristic-zero H¹ on the Lie algebra.
Account for rational splitting of a geometric orbit using finite local H¹ of the centralizer, not the false assertion that a closed embedding gives finitely many rational subgroup orbits.
acceptance: Keep the parent’s recorded erratum about general reductive conjugacy visible; this theorem is a target with the explicit descent gap.

sources.match: The lemma asserts arithmetic G-conjugacy finiteness from complete reducibility, bounded ramification and integral Weil eigenvalues. The planned application assumes integer Frobenius polynomials explicitly and leaves rational orbit splitting and disconnected GO descent as gaps.

nodes.title: Finitely many semisimplification geometries
nodes.statement: Let G be an algebraic group over a characteristic-zero field E with reductive identity component and H⊂G an E-defined G-completely reducible subgroup. Up to the action of Z_G(H)(E), only finitely many E-defined pairs (P,M) occur with P a Richardson parabolic, M a Levi of P and H⊂M. Consequently a fixed completely reducible image gives finitely many parabolic/Levi semisimplification types. This is a finiteness statement up to centralizer conjugacy, not finiteness of actual parabolics.
proofSteps: Choose a maximal E-split torus in Z_G(H) and use conjugacy of maximal E-split tori under Z_G(H)(E) to express allowable E-defined Levi factors by its E-cocharacters.
The finitely many root-weight hyperplanes partition cocharacter space into finitely many faces; use each face to record its parabolic and Levi.
Treat the finite component action without identifying its parabolic with the identity-component parabolic.
acceptance: For H=1 there can be infinitely many actual Borels, but finitely many conjugacy types.

sources.match: The lemmas give finitely many centralizer-conjugacy classes of Levi configurations containing a completely reducible subgroup; root faces also record the finitely many compatible parabolics.

nodes.title: Periods in a single monodromy orbit
nodes.statement: The complex and p-adic period maps of a compatible system, after the stated fibre identifications, lie in one orbit of its differential monodromy group in the relevant compact dual. The orbit is defined by the horizontal tensor relations of the tensor category generated by the connection. Over a nonclosed field use its tensor-isomorphism torsor; do not choose a rational trivialization without an existence argument.
proofSteps: Construct the torsor of horizontal tensor identifications between the variable and reference fibres.
Apply it to the Hodge filtration and use the supplied tensor-isomorphism theorem after algebraic closure; descend the orbit equations.
acceptance: For a constant system the period map is constant.
An arbitrary flag with the right dimensions can violate a horizontal tensor equation.

sources.match: Horizontal tensor identifications put the local period flags in a single differential-monodromy orbit; tensor-isomorphism torsors account for fibre changes.

nodes.title: Parabolic stabilizers of period orbits
nodes.statement: For a polarized pure variation, the stabilizer of its Hodge filtration inside the connected algebraic monodromy group is parabolic; its orbit is consequently projective. Use normality of connected monodromy in the derived generic Mumford–Tate group and the Hodge cocharacter action. Pass to a positive power of the cocharacter if needed to lift the induced inner action; finite disconnected components do not change the connected orbit.
proofSteps: Use the supplied normality theorem to make the Hodge cocharacter act on connected monodromy.
Lift its inner action after a power; identify the stabilizer with the supplied dynamic parabolic.
acceptance: Projectivity is for the connected monodromy orbit, rather than every orbit of a reductive group in a flag space.

sources.match: The Hodge flag stabilizer in monodromy is parabolic, making the connected monodromy orbit projective. The plan exposes the normality and cocharacter inputs used for this conclusion.

nodes.title: Analytic radicals for period ideals
nodes.statement: Let Φ be a local holomorphic period map in smooth coordinates at x and I the ideal of convergent germs defining Φ⁻¹(Z). If an algebraic function g on the smooth base vanishes on that germ, some power g^m lies in I. Obtain this exact membership statement from the local analytic Nullstellensatz in ComplexComparisonPartII C0; the general theorem I(V(I))=√I is a requested supplier extension, not a second construction here.
proofSteps: Apply the requested analytic Nullstellensatz to the finitely generated period ideal in C{z₁,…,z_n}.
Use radical membership to choose a finite exponent m and convergent coefficient germs; retain those coefficients for the formal transfer.
acceptance: For I=(z²), z vanishes on V(I) but need not belong to I; the radical is essential.

nodes.title: Algebraic degeneracy from period codimension
nodes.statement: Let X be smooth irreducible over C of positive dimension d and let its pure polarized integral variation have connected monodromy period orbit D_mon. If an algebraic subset Z⊂D_mon has codimension at least d, every positive-dimensional irreducible analytic component of the inverse image of Z under a local period map is contained in a proper algebraic subvariety of X. Zero-dimensional local components are points and are also proper. The assertion is componentwise or germwise; it does not assert that infinitely many components have one common proper algebraic closure.
proofSteps: Apply the externally owned pure integral period-map Ax–Schanuel theorem to the graph of the period map and X×Z.
The codimension inequality forces each component to be atypical unless its base projection is algebraically degenerate; handle isolated points separately.
acceptance: Require positive dim X.
Use integral polarized pure variations, the actual scope of the cited Ax–Schanuel input; no unproved mixed or nonintegral extension is claimed.

sources.match: The period-map Ax–Schanuel argument makes components over a sufficiently high-codimension algebraic flag locus algebraically degenerate. The plan uses the pure polarized integral scope of the external theorem.

nodes.title: Transfer to p-adic non-density
nodes.statement: Let X/Q be smooth geometrically connected of positive dimension d, with a pure polarized integral compatible system, and fix a smooth p-adic residue disk Ω and its monodromy period orbit. For an algebraic Z in that orbit of codimension at least d, Φ_p⁻¹(Z)∩Ω is not Zariski dense in X. After shrinking to affinoid subdisks the assertion combines finitely many minimal primes; finitely many residue disks combine by taking a product of nonzero algebraic equations.
proofSteps: Transfer formal Taylor expansions through an abstract field isomorphism Q̄_p≅C; no continuity of this isomorphism is needed or asserted.
For each local analytic component, complex degeneracy provides a nonzero algebraic equation; the analytic Nullstellensatz places a power in the period ideal.
Descend that equation through a finite coefficient extension using its norm, then descend finite linear systems to the coefficient field.
Use Krull intersection in the localized Tate algebra at each prime to pass from every formal order to genuine ideal membership.
The Noetherian Tate algebra has finitely many minimal primes; multiply their nonzero algebraic equations and use injectivity of the germ map on irreducible X.
acceptance: Formal vanishing alone is not analytic ideal membership without Krull intersection.
An infinite union of separately nondense subsets need not be nondense; only the finite component/disk decomposition is used.

sources.match: Complex degeneracy is transferred through formal expansions, analytic radical membership and Krull intersection to p-adic non-density. Finite minimal-prime decomposition is essential to obtaining one proper algebraic locus.

nodes.title: Index classes of subdirect monodromy
nodes.statement: Let H be a connected semisimple characteristic-zero group with simple adjoint quotient and let L⊂H^I be a closed subgroup surjective onto each factor, for finite nonempty I. Put i~j when the projection to factors i,j is not the full product, allowing the equivalent graph-of-an-isogeny formulation after central quotients. This is an equivalence relation. Projection onto one representative of each class is surjective with finite kernel. Apply to SL_N (N≥2), Sp_2r (r≥1), and SO_N (N=3 or N≥5); SO₂ and SO₄ require separate treatment and are excluded.
proofSteps: Apply the simple-adjoint Goursat lemma to each two-factor projection.
Use a triple projection to prove transitivity, then induct on the number of classes.
acceptance: Geometric hypersurface applications have N≥6.

sources.match: A subdirect product of simple-adjoint classical factors has classes of diagonally dependent coordinates and finitely many independent representatives. The plan excludes SO2 and SO4 from this simple-adjoint statement.

nodes.title: Strongly balanced monodromy
nodes.statement: For the preceding index partition and integer c≥1, c-balanced means all classes have equal cardinality and there are at least c classes. Given a permutation σ of I, strongly c-balanced additionally means σ preserves the partition and every σ-orbit meets at least c distinct classes. For a subgroup of the coefficient group, apply this condition to its intersection with the product of derived classical factors after algebraic closure. Neither the scalar centres nor the similitude characters supply the independent directions.

Use the derived-factor interpretation to compare with the coefficient-group formulation.

nodes.statement: For a nonconstant-up-to-translation family of primitive smooth ample hypersurfaces satisfying the supplied classical-monodromy hypotheses, the orbit character supplied by SC.8 can be chosen so that its coefficient cohomology system has strongly c-balanced differential monodromy relative to residue Frobenius, for any prescribed c≥1. Use the algebraically closed extension comparison to return to the de Rham group.

nodes.title: Codimension of semisimple isomorphism orbits
nodes.statement: Let a uniform coefficient filtration have single-factor profile h and strongly c-balanced monodromy relative to σ. Suppose E^σ=E₀ on the chosen Frobenius cycle, e>0 and A≥(e+dim H)/c. In the monodromy flag orbit, the locus whose filtered Frobenius module is isomorphic to a prescribed one has codimension at least e. More generally select one σ-cycle meeting c index classes; one factor dimension dim H is the centralizer cost for that cycle.

The product flag dimension is cA, while semilinear centralizer orbits have dimension at most dim H.
Take the smooth homogeneous projection back to the full monodromy orbit.

sources.match: Uniform Hodge flags and a long enough independent Frobenius cycle force a prescribed isomorphism orbit to have the stated codimension after the single-factor centralizer cost.

nodes.title: Non-density for semisimple integral fibres
nodes.statement: Let 𝓧 be of finite type over Z[S⁻¹] with smooth geometrically connected generic fibre X of positive dimension. For an integral polarized pure compatible system with integral Frobenius and rational Frobenius characteristic polynomials outside S, uniform coefficient filtration and strongly c-balanced monodromy, assume A≥(dim X+dim H)/c. The integral points whose global coefficient-group representations are G-completely reducible are not Zariski dense in X. Fix the coefficient permutation representation and enlarge S only by finitely many primes.
proofSteps: Global finiteness leaves finitely many semisimple G-representations.
On each of finitely many residue disks a fixed representation gives a centralizer orbit of filtrations; apply the codimension bound with e=dim X.
Apply p-adic transfer and take the finite union.
acceptance: This is restricted to semisimple integral fibres; the all-points assertion requires the balanced associated-graded argument.

sources.match: Arithmetic finiteness and the preceding codimension estimate combine with p-adic transcendence to exclude density of points with completely reducible fibre representations.

nodes.title: Central weights of filtrations
nodes.statement: For a characteristic-zero algebraic group S with reductive identity component, let a_S=X_*(Z(S°)°)⊗Q, equivalently the Q-dual of X^*(S°)⊗Q via the central pairing. Compute these geometric character spaces after algebraic closure and retain their Galois action for descent; rational cocharacters give invariant classes. The weight w_S(μ) of a rational cocharacter μ is its projection to a_S. For a Levi M⊂G, restriction of rational characters gives a canonical inclusion ι_GM:a_G→a_M and a splitting of the opposite projection. proofSteps: Use the root decomposition to split the central and derived rational cocharacter spaces.

nodes.title: Filtrations induced on a Levi quotient
nodes.statement: Let G be as in M2.2, P a Richardson parabolic with Levi quotient M and F a G-filtration. Choose a splitting cocharacter of F taking values in P; its projection defines a filtration F_M independent of this choice. Put Q=P_μ, the stabilizer of F. On each Q-homogeneous orbit Q·x in a flag variety, its μ-fixed points are conjugate under Z_Q(μ); use this for the Q-orbit of the point representing P to establish independence. For GL(V), F_M is the filtration induced by F on the graded vector space of the P-flag.
proofSteps: Place a maximal torus of the filtration stabilizer in P after conjugacy, giving a splitting in P.
Compare two P-valued choices inside the Q-homogeneous orbit Q·P in G/P, using the fixed-point lemma for Q=P_μ. Their Levi projections differ by the subgroup fixing the induced filtration.
Identify the construction on each representation with the associated-graded filtration.
acceptance: Independence concerns filtrations, rather than literal equality of chosen cocharacters.

nodes.title: Balanced, weakly balanced and semibalanced filtrations
nodes.statement: For F and P→M as above, F is balanced when w_M(F_M)=ι_GM(w_G(F)); weakly balanced when ⟨γ_P,F_M⟩=0; and semibalanced when ⟨γ_P,F_M⟩≤0. Balance implies weak balance, which implies semibalance. The latter two test one modular character and are generally weaker than the vector identity defining balance. The restriction to G° preserves all three conditions.
proofSteps: Pair the vector balance identity with γ_P, which vanishes on the centre of G.
Verify the modular sign on block triangular matrices and compare with weight averages on each graded block.
acceptance: The sign is ≤0 for the inverse-determinant convention.

nodes.title: Global purity forces balance over Q
nodes.statement: Let ρ:G_Q→G(Q_p) be crystalline at p, pure of integral Weil weight w on the chosen faithful representation, with image contained in P. The de Rham Hodge filtration induced on the corresponding inner Levi quotient is balanced relative to P. In the GL case this says every global graded subquotient has Hodge–Tate average w/2, using the convention that a Tate object of geometric Frobenius q has de Rham weight 1. This global assertion is over Q; it is false in this form for arbitrary number fields with different embeddings.
proofSteps: Apply the parent global pure-character weight theorem to all rational characters of the Levi that are trivial on Z(G).
Translate the resulting weight-zero identities into the central-weight equality.
Track the inner form under D_cris so P and its Levi are transported rather than identified without comparison.

nodes.title: Bifiltered Frobenius objects and graded types
nodes.statement: A bifiltered coefficient Frobenius object is (V,φ,F,f), with Hodge G-filtration F, φ-stable auxiliary G-filtration f and the given semilinear coefficient structure. Its graded type is the G-conjugacy class of (P_f,φ_M,F_M). Forget the numerical indexing of f when defining this type, while retaining the full Hodge indexing of F_M. This forgotten auxiliary indexing is necessary for finiteness; types are not unfiltered characteristic polynomials.
proofSteps: Use the φ-stable parabolic of f and project φ and F to the Levi quotient.
Form conjugacy classes of these quotient data with all defining coefficient tensors.
acceptance: Auxiliary reindexing changes f as an indexed filtration but does not change its graded type.

sources.match: An auxiliary Frobenius-stable filtration and a Hodge filtration give an associated-graded filtered Frobenius object. Its type forgets the auxiliary grading labels while retaining Hodge degrees and classical tensors.

nodes.title: Finite cyclic cocycles in unipotent groups
nodes.statement: Let U be a characteristic-zero unipotent algebraic group and ψ an automorphism of finite order dividing r≥1. If uψ(u)⋯ψ^(r−1)(u)=1, there is v∈U with u=v⁻¹ψ(v). Thus H¹(C_r,U)=1 for this action. The finite-order condition on ψ is essential to this argument.
proofSteps: Induct along a ψ-stable central series with vector-group quotients.
On a vector quotient use the averaging homotopy, dividing by r; lift the correction and continue in the central kernel.
acceptance: For U additive the cocycle relation is the norm-zero relation, which equals the image of ψ−1 in characteristic zero.

sources.match: A norm-one cocycle for a finite-order automorphism of a characteristic-zero unipotent group is a coboundary, by induction through its central quotients.

nodes.title: Levi factors stable under semisimple Frobenius
nodes.statement: If a semisimple element φ of the ambient characteristic-zero group normalizes the connected parabolic P, a unipotent conjugate of a chosen Levi of P is φ-stable. In the norm argument choose r killing the induced finite component action. The relevant cocycle u lies in Z_U(φ^r), where conjugation by φ has order dividing r; do not assume conjugation has finite order on all of U.
proofSteps: Write φ relative to a Levi and its unipotent radical and derive the norm relation.
Use that φ is semisimple and the norm relation to place the correction in Z_U(φ^r).
Apply finite cyclic unipotent cocycle vanishing on this fixed subgroup and conjugate the Levi.
acceptance: A diagonal semisimple matrix can act on a unipotent root group by an eigenvalue of infinite order.

sources.match: A semisimple element in a parabolic preserves a Levi factor. The plan repairs the cyclic argument by restricting the radical to the centralizer of a suitable power before invoking the finite-order cocycle lemma.

nodes.title: Finitely many local types from global semisimplification
nodes.statement: For fixed global coefficient-group semisimplification ρ^ss and fixed residue Frobenius data, the local bifiltered objects obtained by choosing a global semisimplification flag have only finitely many graded types, and their induced Hodge filtrations are balanced. The assertion concerns the quotient type forgetting auxiliary flag indices. It does not say there are finitely many flags or extensions.

Apply crystalline comparison to the fixed global quotient representation and global purity to its Hodge weights.
Use unipotent conjugacy and the stable-Levi step to compare different splittings without changing the type.
acceptance: Infinitely many auxiliary indexings do not introduce spurious infinitely many types.

sources.match: After forgetting auxiliary indices, local graded types arising from one fixed global semisimplification form a finite set, using the finite centralizer-orbit classification.

nodes.title: Root pairing for opposite flag directions
nodes.statement: Fix positive roots Σ⁺ and standard parabolics P,Q containing the positive Borel; let Σ_P,Σ_Q be their full Lie root sets, and Δ_P,Δ_Q the simple roots of their Levis. For w with w⁻¹Δ_P⊂Σ⁺ and wΔ_Q⊂Σ⁺, the map β↦−wβ bijects {β∈Σ\Σ_Q : wβ>0} with {α∈Σ\Σ_P : w⁻¹α>0}; its inverse is α↦−w⁻¹α. Each set has size length(w). The two sign equivalences are β∈Σ\Σ_Q ⇒ (wβ>0 iff −wβ∉Σ_P) and the analogous statement with P,Q,w⁻¹.
proofSteps: Write tangent dimensions as the root spaces in Lie(U)/(Lie(U)∩Lie(Q)).
Use minimality of w to identify the two root sets and check the forward and inverse maps explicitly.
Pair the root sums with the Hodge cocharacter, using the inverse-determinant sign fixed earlier.
acceptance: Check rank-one SL₂ directly and a noninvolutive Weyl element of SL₃ so w and w⁻¹ cannot be interchanged.

nodes.title: Semibalanced fixed-graded fibre bound
nodes.statement: Let G=H^c over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, with H connected reductive of rank t, and let F₀ have uniform single-factor adjoint profile h. Put A=Σ_(a>0)h^a and B=Σ_(a>0)a h^a. For an integer e>0, assume A≥e/c and B>T(e/c)+T((h⁰−t)/2+e/c), with both T arguments in its domain. For every parabolic P and every prescribed induced Levi filtration, its semibalanced fibre inside the orbit G·F₀ has codimension at least e. In the single connected group case, the stronger LV hypotheses A≥e and B>T(e)+T(h⁰/2+e) give codimension strictly greater than e for balanced fibres.
proofSteps: Stratify by finitely many P–Q double cosets and compute the dimension of each induced-Levi fibre.
Translate semibalance to a nonpositive modular sum; pair its root contributions by the preceding bijection.
The largest e/c root weights and the central zero-weight correction cost at most the two displayed top sums.
Strict failure of the second inequality would be necessary for a stratum of codimension below e, giving the contradiction.
acceptance: The zero-weight correction is (h⁰−rank H)/2 in LS, whereas the weaker LV bound uses h⁰/2.
Track ≥ in the dimension conclusion separately from the strict numerical inequality.

sources.match: A root-stratified dimension estimate bounds semibalanced filtrations with fixed induced Levi data. The stronger LS version subtracts the rank in its zero-weight correction.

nodes.title: Dimension of Frobenius-stable graded pairs
nodes.statement: Fix a semisimple Frobenius φ in the algebraic coefficient normalizer. Pairs (P,F_M) with φ∈P and prescribed conjugacy class of the quotient filtered Frobenius data form finitely many centralizer orbits, hence have dimension at most dim Z_G(φ). For an arbitrary φ replace it by φ^ss and use φ-stable Levi reduction; the resulting dimension bound uses dim Z_G(φ^ss). Apply cyclewise to bound the cost by dim H.
proofSteps: Conjugate to a φ-stable Levi, then fix its quotient conjugacy data.
Use the finite parabolic/Levi classification to leave finitely many choices modulo Z_G(φ^ss).
Bound each orbit by the dimension of its acting centralizer, not by the number of its rational points.
acceptance: Replacing φ by φ^ss can enlarge the centralizer and therefore gives a valid upper bound.

nodes.title: Fixed-type codimension under balanced monodromy
nodes.statement: Let the coefficient system have uniform single-factor profile h, rank t for H, strongly c-balanced monodromy and a balanced reference graded type. Given a positive integer e, assume A≥(e+dim H)/c and B>T((e+dim H)/c)+T((h⁰−t)/2+(e+dim H)/c), with valid T arguments. In the monodromy period orbit, the locus admitting a φ-stable auxiliary filtration with that graded type has codimension at least e.
proofSteps: Balance makes the total modular weight zero; select a Frobenius cycle with nonpositive average modular weight.
Choose c independent index-class representatives in that cycle and project smoothly to their flag product.
Apply the semibalanced fixed-graded bound with parameter e+dim H.
Allow the graded pairs to vary; their dimension costs at most dim H by the semilinear centralizer bound.
acceptance: Both inequalities use the one-factor T_H, rather than a T for the whole restriction-of-scalars group.

sources.match: The fixed-graded estimate is applied to independent factors in one Frobenius cycle, then the varying graded-pair cost is subtracted to obtain the prescribed codimension.

nodes.title: The coefficient non-density theorem
nodes.statement: Let 𝓧 be of finite type over Z[S⁻¹] with smooth geometrically connected generic fibre X of dimension d>0. Let V be a pure polarized integral Hodge–Deligne system with integral Frobenius and rational Frobenius characteristic polynomials outside S, an equidimensional E-module of classical rank N and the required coefficient pairing. Assume a uniform factor profile h, strongly c-balanced differential monodromy relative to residue Frobenius and, writing t=rank H, A≥(d+dim H)/c and B>T((d+dim H)/c)+T((h⁰−t)/2+(d+dim H)/c). All T arguments must be in [0,dim H]. Then 𝓧(Z[S⁻¹]) is not Zariski dense in X. No semisimplicity hypothesis is imposed on the actual fibres.
proofSteps: There are finitely many global G-semisimplifications by arithmetic finiteness.
For each residue disk and each global type, the finite local graded-type reduction supplies balanced types.
Apply the codimension theorem with e=d, followed by p-adic period non-density.
The integral point set lies in a finite union of the resulting proper algebraic subsets.
acceptance: Keep separate the finite list of semisimplifications and the possibly infinitely many nonsemisimple representations.

sources.match: The theorem combines finite global semisimplifications, balanced graded types and strong monodromy balance to prove non-density without requiring the original representations to split. The plan explicitly adds the rational Frobenius-polynomial interface needed by arithmetic finiteness.

nodes.title: Comparing crystalline and forgetful fibre functors
nodes.statement: For the neutral tensor category generated by a crystalline p-adic representation V with its intersection/similitude tensors, the forgetful fibre functor and underlying D_cris fibre functor become tensor-isomorphic over Q̄_p. Such an isomorphism identifies their Tannaka groups by conjugacy and preserves every defining pairing tensor. This is an existence statement over the algebraic closure, not a canonical rational comparison.
proofSteps: Apply the generic tensor-isomorphism torsor theorem to this proven neutral category.
Finite tensor generation makes the relevant torsor finite type, so it has an algebraically closed point.
Transport all intersection and multiplier tensors through the chosen point.
acceptance: An arbitrary linear isomorphism of the two vector spaces need not respect the forms.

sources.match: The tensor-isomorphism argument compares crystalline and underlying fibre functors over an algebraic closure and preserves the intersection tensors. It supplies existence, not a canonical rational identification.

nodes.title: The Hodge torus in the Galois image
nodes.statement: For primitive middle cohomology of a smooth projective variety over Q_p with good reduction, transport the Hodge cocharacter through the crystalline/forgetful tensor comparison. The Zariski closure of the local p-adic Galois image contains a torus conjugate over Q̄_p to the Hodge torus. Apply the tensor-compatible Sen/Wintenberger splitting supplied by R06.2; its compatibility with defining form tensors upgrades the GL assertion to the full similitude group.
proofSteps: Use the common tensor-compatible Hodge–Tate splitting to construct the cocharacter in the algebraic Galois group.
Use fibre comparison to identify its conjugacy class with the de Rham Hodge cocharacter.
Levi projection preserves its torus conjugacy class by the semisimplification torus lemma.
acceptance: Do not infer the similitude-group assertion from equality of underlying GL weight multiplicities alone.

sources.match: The proof uses the Hodge–Tate splitting to place the Hodge torus in the algebraic Galois image; the footnote explains compatibility with the full similitude tensors.

nodes.title: A bounded prime with small Frobenius centralizer
nodes.statement: For a fixed smooth projective family over Z[S⁻¹], with fixed primitive middle-cohomology Hodge type and group GAut of the intersection pairing, there is L such that every integral fibre admits a prime ℓ≤L outside S with dim Z_GAut((φ_crys,ℓ)^ss)≤h⁰. Choose an auxiliary prime p outside S large enough for the common shifted Fontaine–Laffaille interval. The bound is uniform in the integral point, not an effective formula for L.
proofSteps: Finitely many auxiliary-p semisimplifications remain by the parent GL finiteness theorem.
In each reductive image choose a very regular open subset avoiding its finitely many nontrivial root-weight equalities; Chebotarev supplies one prime per class.
The Hodge torus in the image bounds the centralizer dimension by h⁰.
Use the externally supplied Katz–Messing polynomial equality and multiplier ℓ^r for middle degree r to transfer the dimension bound to crystalline cohomology at ℓ.
acceptance: Equal Frobenius characteristic polynomials determine the geometric centralizer dimension in the classical form group; no uniqueness of rational conjugacy is asserted.

sources.match: Finite global representation types and Chebotarev select uniformly bounded primes whose semisimple crystalline centralizer has dimension bounded by h0; Katz–Messing transfers the characteristic-polynomial data.

nodes.title: Bad self-dual filtrations have large codimension
nodes.statement: For a classical similitude space V, Frobenius φ and prescribed filtered Frobenius graded objects of a φ-stable self-dual auxiliary flag, put z=dim Z_GAut(φ^ss). Require each nonzero graded object to have Hodge-weight average r/2, and set e>0. If A≥z+e and B>T(z+e)+T(h⁰/2+z+e), with valid T arguments, the self-dual Hodge filtrations admitting such a flag have codimension at least e in their fixed Hodge-type flag variety. Self-dual middle pieces retain their pairing tensor.
proofSteps: Reduce to semisimple φ, which only enlarges the relevant incidence locus.
Stratify by finitely many conjugacy types of self-dual flags; graded-pair variation costs at most z.
Apply the connected balanced fixed-graded estimate with parameter z+e, then project the incidence locus to the Hodge flag variety.
acceptance: Use A≥z+e as printed in the published article, not the unnecessarily strict inequality in arXiv v3.

sources.match: The proposition removes self-dual graded Frobenius configurations under two adjoint inequalities. The published first inequality is non-strict, and its centralizer parameter is the dimension of the semisimple centralizer.

nodes.title: Classical semisimplification fibres are nondense
nodes.statement: Under the two numerical inequalities of the following theorem, fix ℓ∉S and a residue point with crystalline semisimple centralizer dimension at most h⁰. Integral points in its residue disk whose global ℓ-adic representations have a prescribed semisimplification form a nondense subset of the base. Global semisimplification flags are self-dual after pairing dual constituents, and each graded Hodge average is r/2 by global purity over Q.
proofSteps: Construct paired self-dual semisimplification flags and transport their graded data through D_cris.
Use the small centralizer and the bad-filtration bound with e=dim Y.
Apply the common p-adic transfer theorem on the disk.
acceptance: Actual representations may be nonsplit; only their global semisimplifications are fixed.

sources.match: For a fixed global semisimplification and a suitable residue disk, purity forces the graded Hodge-average condition and the bad-filtration bound yields non-density.

nodes.title: Higher-dimensional integral-point non-density
nodes.statement: Let 𝓨 be smooth of finite type over Z[S⁻¹], and let π:𝓩→𝓨 be smooth projective with geometrically connected relative dimension r, a relative ample class, and smooth geometrically connected generic base Y/Q of dimension d>0. Let V be primitive degree-r cohomology and assume the Zariski closure of geometric monodromy contains Aut(V,⟨,⟩)°, the identity component of the isometry group. Its adjoint profile is still computed in the similitude group GAut(V,⟨,⟩). For its adjoint profile require A≥h⁰+d and B>T(h⁰+d)+T(3h⁰/2+d), with valid T arguments. Then 𝓨(Z[S⁻¹]) is not Zariski dense in Y. The theorem is the classical first instance of the shared period/codimension mechanism; the bounded-prime step is distinct from the coefficient-orbit construction.
proofSteps: Choose finitely many possible small-centralizer primes using the bounded-prime lemma.
For each prime, parent arithmetic finiteness leaves finitely many semisimplifications and finitely many residue disks.
Apply the preceding nondensity theorem to each resulting fibre and take their finite union.
acceptance: This theorem gives nondensity without assuming full monodromy on subvarieties.
For an elliptic family, geometric monodromy may be Sp₂=SL₂ while the similitude group is GSp₂=GL₂. The monodromy hypothesis must not demand the scalar similitude direction.

sources.locator: Theorem 10.1, pp. 969–970, monodromy hypothesis (10.1), p. 968; proofs §§10.3–10.5, pp. 975–982
sources.match: The theorem assumes the full connected primitive isometry group in geometric monodromy and two numerical adjoint inequalities; the proof combines finitely many bounded primes, global types and residue disks.

nodes.title: Finiteness under monodromy on every subvariety
nodes.statement: In the preceding setup, assume every positive-dimensional geometrically irreducible subvariety of Y retains the full connected primitive isometry monodromy after passage to its smooth locus and finite field of definition, with the required rational arithmetic model or restriction-of-scalars comparison. Then the integral point set is finite. This stronger monodromy condition is an additional hypothesis; it is not established for the universal hypersurface family by large generic monodromy alone.
proofSteps: Apply nondensity on every positive-dimensional irreducible component of the closure of the integral points, over its field of definition with the specified arithmetic comparison.
Use Noetherian induction on the proper closed subsets until only zero-dimensional components remain.
acceptance: A family with a positive-dimensional isotrivial subvariety does not meet this stronger hypothesis.

sources.match: The final clause upgrades non-density to finiteness if full monodromy persists on every positive-dimensional subvariety. This plan states the extra number-field arithmetic comparison needed when taking closure components.

nodes.title: A point-count bound for Frobenius centralizers
nodes.statement: For a smooth degree-d hypersurface of dimension n≥2 over F_q, let b>0 be the dimension of primitive middle cohomology. For every integer N≥1 satisfying q^((n/2+1)·2N)<b/3, the GL-centralizer of semisimple Frobenius has dimension at most 3b²/N. Thus the largest such positive N gives the strongest stated estimate whenever one exists. The assertion is independent of the bounded-prime argument and is not used to claim a computable universal prime bound.
proofSteps: Normalize Frobenius eigenvalues onto the unit circle using purity and identify centralizer dimension with the sum of squared eigenvalue multiplicities.
Use the squared Dirichlet kernel with frequencies −2N,…,2N and coefficients 2N+1−|j| to bound this sum by its weighted power sums.

Use the complete-intersection trace identity to cancel the ambient P^n terms. The elementary bounds 0≤#Y(F_(q^j))≤#P^(n+1)(F_(q^j)) imply |Σ_s(λ_s/q^(n/2))^j|≤q^((n/2+1)j). Apply this through frequency 2N and the displayed cutoff; sum the geometric series to obtain the constant 3.
acceptance: N=0 is excluded.
The exponent 2N is required because squaring the kernel doubles its Fourier support.

sources.locator: Lemma 12.1 and proof, pp. 995–996, corrected Fourier cutoff
sources.match: The squared-kernel estimate bounds eigenvalue multiplicities, hence semisimple Frobenius centralizer dimension. The plan strengthens the cutoff to cover frequency 2N, correcting the extracted source error.

nodes.title: Classical adjoint profiles from Eulerian multiplicities
nodes.statement: For smooth ample hypersurfaces in an n-dimensional abelian variety, n≥2 and normalized degree d>0, import m_q=d·A(n,q), 0≤q<n, and N=n!d from SC.3. The adjoint weights of GL_N, GSp_N or GO_N are obtained from End(V), Sym²(V) or ∧²(V), with the scalar multiplier direction in degree zero for the similitude groups. For the geometric parity choices GL in either parity, GSp when n is even and GO when n is odd, 2h⁰<dim H+rank H. In particular (h⁰−rank H)/2<A. The opposite, nongeometric parity choices are not part of this assertion.
proofSteps: Compute zero-weight multiplicities: for GL use Σm_q²; for GSp use (Σm_q²+m_mid)/2+1; for GO use (Σm_q²−m_mid)/2+1, where m_mid=0 if there is no central index.
Combine the Eulerian convolution estimate below with the explicit dimensions and ranks, retaining the strict rank correction.
acceptance: For n=2,d=1, m=(1,1); GL₂ and GSp₂ satisfy the assertion, while arbitrary GO₂ is not the geometric pairing case.

sources.match: The lemma compares classical adjoint positive weights with the zero-weight and rank terms using Eulerian multiplicities. The plan restricts the form groups to geometric pairing parity to exclude the GO2 counterexample.

nodes.title: Difference distribution of Eulerian weights
nodes.statement: For n≥2 define α_q=A(n,q)/n!, extended by zero outside 0≤q<n, and β_j=Σ_q α_q α_(q−j), j∈Z. This is the distribution of the difference of two independent ascent counts, not of their sum without recentering. It is a symmetric, finitely supported probability distribution and is the normalized GL adjoint multiplicity profile.
proofSteps: Import Eulerian numbers and their permutation-count interpretation from their combinatorial owner.
Form the finite convolution with reflected index and prove normalization by a double sum.
acceptance: Changing q−j to j−q is harmless only after proving symmetry of the individual Eulerian distribution.

sources.match: The adjoint multiplicities are the convolution of the Eulerian ascent law with its reflected law, which is the distribution of a difference of two independent counts.

nodes.title: The central Eulerian convolution mass is at most one half

nodes.title: Primitive hypersurface Hodge numbers from the Jacobian ring
nodes.statement: For a smooth degree-d hypersurface in P^n over C with n≥2 and d≥2, the primitive middle Hodge multiplicity h^{p,n−1−p} equals the coefficient of t^((p+1)d−n−1) in (1+t+⋯+t^(d−2))^(n+1), for 0≤p<n. proofSteps: Specialize the toric residue construction to the Cox ring C[x₀,…,x_n], with degree class d and anticanonical degree n+1.
Smoothness makes the partial derivatives a homogeneous regular sequence; its Hilbert series is (1−t^(d−1))^(n+1)/(1−t)^(n+1).
Use residue Hodge degree and symmetry to obtain the displayed coefficient.

nodes.title: Eulerian asymptotics of projective hypersurface cohomology
nodes.statement: Fix n≥2. As d→∞, primitive h^{p,n−1−p}(d)∼d^n A(n,p)/n! for 0≤p<n. After adjoint formation, h^a/(d^(2n)/2)→β_a for the orthogonal or symplectic similitude group. The universal parameter space has dimension binomial(n+d,d)−1=O(d^n), hence dim Y/h⁰→0. Here n is ambient dimension; the hypersurface dimension is n−1.
proofSteps: Expand the coefficient formula by inclusion–exclusion; its leading d^n coefficient is the Eulerian finite-difference formula.
Compute adjoint multiplicities from symmetric/exterior squares; diagonal terms and the scalar direction have lower order.
Compare the parameter-space growth O(d^n) with adjoint h⁰ of order d^(2n).

nodes.title: Normal-limit estimates for adjoint Eulerian weights
nodes.statement: As n→∞ the centered ascent count divided by √n converges in law to N(0,1/12); its independent difference converges to N(0,1/6). Consequently Σ_(a>0)aβ_a≥C√n for some C>0 and all sufficiently large n. Log-concavity and the variance imply β₀<40/√n for sufficiently large n. For each fixed c>0 the sum of the largest c/√n fraction of difference weights is o(√n).
proofSteps: Import the Eulerian central limit theorem from its common combinatorial/probabilistic supplier rather than reproving that theorem here.
Use bounded second moments for uniform integrability of the first moment.
Combine log-concavity with the variance bound for the central-mass estimate; control the upper-tail partial sum by Cauchy–Schwarz.
acceptance: Convergence in distribution alone does not imply convergence of unbounded first moments; include uniform integrability.

The positive first moment has size √n, while each discarded top fraction of order 1/√n has sum o(√n).
Choose n large for a strict numerical margin; then choose d large so the asymptotic errors and dim Y/h⁰ preserve that margin.

nodes.title: Good reduction and primitive hypersurfaces
nodes.statement: Fix a number field K, finite S, an abelian variety A/K with abelian scheme model 𝓐 over O_K[S⁻¹], and a smooth ample effective divisor H⊂A. Good reduction outside S means its schematic closure in 𝓐 is smooth over O_K[S⁻¹]. The translation stabilizer Stab(H) is the finite group scheme of a with H+a=H; H is primitive when Stab(H)(K̄)={0}. Only nonzero translations are excluded, since translation by zero always fixes H.
proofSteps: Use the abelian scheme and schematic closure with their canonical translation action.
Represent the stabilizer as the fibre of the Hilbert orbit map; ampleness implies finiteness, and characteristic zero makes it reduced.
acceptance: For a∈A(K), properness extends a over O_K[S⁻¹], so its translation preserves good reduction.

nodes.title: Reducing a dense arithmetic closure to a smooth base
nodes.statement: Let a set of integral points in a finite-type characteristic-zero parameter scheme be Zariski dense in an irreducible component C of its closure. Resolve C properly by X→C, isomorphic over a dense smooth open U. The points in U have unique rational lifts, and after spreading out the proper map these lifts are integral by the valuative criterion. They are dense in X. Points outside U are handled through the finitely many closure components or Noetherian induction, rather than by assuming every rational point of C lifts.

Use density to retain a dense subset of the integral points in that open.

nodes.title: Nonconstant abelian-divisor families are arithmetically nondense

Choose c using the Eulerian numerical criterion and then use SC.8’s conjugate-uniform torsion orbit to construct the compatible coefficient system.
proofSteps: Choose a good p and a torsion character of order prime to p with all required conjugate monodromy properties.
Construct the orbit coefficient system, its integral lattice, polarization, uniform Eulerian profile and strong c-balance.
Apply the coefficient non-density theorem to this positive-dimensional base.

nodes.title: Primitive hypersurface Shafarevich finiteness
nodes.statement: For A/K, good reduction outside S and fixed ample class φ, primitive smooth hypersurfaces in class φ with good reduction outside S form finitely many geometric translation classes when n≥4, or when n=3 and d=φ³/6 is not an exceptional D_j, j≥1. Translation orbits in the divisor parameter scheme are closed because A is proper. Hence an irreducible component containing a dense arithmetic set either lies in one orbit or contradicts the nontranslation-family theorem.
proofSteps: Take the irreducible components of the arithmetic closure and apply the smooth-base reduction.
If the generic family is not translation constant, nondensity contradicts density of its lifted integral parameters.
If it is translation constant, the closed translation orbit contains the whole component, including its boundary.
There are finitely many components and therefore finitely many geometric translation classes.
acceptance: Closedness of the proper orbit accounts for boundary points without assuming that a dense open exhausts the component.

nodes.title: Finite stabilizers and primitive isogeny quotients
nodes.statement: Every smooth ample hypersurface H in A is the inverse image of a primitive smooth ample divisor H′ in A/T, where T=Stab(H) is finite and the quotient isogeny has degree |T|. Its normalized degree satisfies d(H)=|T|d(H′). For fixed numerical class, only finitely many possible kernels T occur: their orders divide d(H), and each lies in the finite torsion subgroup A[m] for a common multiple m. Descent of the quotient and H′ is over K.
proofSteps: Use finite flat quotient and descent of a T-invariant Cartier divisor along the characteristic-zero étale isogeny.
Use the projection formula to compare top self-intersections.
Bound the group orders by d and embed all kernels into A[m], leaving finitely many subgroup schemes.
acceptance: A fixed order permits finitely many subgroup schemes of the fixed finite torsion group, not finitely many arbitrary finite group schemes.

nodes.title: From geometric translations to A(K)-translations
nodes.statement: For a fixed K-defined smooth ample divisor H with finite stabilizer T, K-defined geometric translates are parameterized by (A/T)(K) inside its orbit. Their A(K)-translation classes inject into (A/T)(K)/πA(K), a finite group by weak Mordell–Weil for the isogeny π. For primitive H, T=0 and geometric translation between two K-defined divisors is uniquely K-rational. Thus a finite list of geometric translation classes gives a finite list modulo A(K).
proofSteps: Identify the proper orbit with A/T and its K-points.
Choose an integer m such that [m] on A/T factors through π; the quotient by πA(K) is a quotient of the finite weak-Mordell–Weil group modulo m.
For primitive H use uniqueness of the translating point to descend directly by Galois invariance.
acceptance: For nonprimitive H a rational orbit point need not lift to A(K); finite isogeny cokernel, rather than surjectivity, is the correct statement.

nodes.title: Shafarevich finiteness for all smooth ample hypersurfaces

An exceptional quotient degree D_j would force D_j to divide d, excluded by hypothesis.
Pull back the finite lists and use rational translation descent.

Return from geometric translations to A(K)-translations by rational descent.
